Grade 7 Science Lesson Plan: Photosynthesis

Lesson Overview

Grade: 7  |  Subject: Life Science  |  Duration: 60 minutes

Topic: How plants make food: photosynthesis, its inputs and outputs, and why it matters to all living things.

Prior knowledge: Basic plant parts (roots, stem, leaves), the idea that living things need energy, and the difference between a reactant and a product (introduced informally).

Learning Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students will be able to:

  1. State the purpose of photosynthesis: to convert light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose (sugar).
  2. Identify the reactants (carbon dioxide, water, light energy) and the products (glucose, oxygen) of photosynthesis.
  3. Describe where photosynthesis happens in a plant (leaves, chloroplasts containing chlorophyll) and how each reactant enters the plant.
  4. Explain how photosynthesis supports other living things through food and oxygen.
  5. Predict how changing a factor such as light affects the rate of photosynthesis.

Materials

Whole class

  • Projector or whiteboard with a photosynthesis diagram (sun, leaf, roots, CO2, H2O, O2, glucose)
  • A healthy potted plant (to show leaves and stomata discussion)
  • Word wall cards: photosynthesis, chlorophyll, chloroplast, stomata, glucose, reactant, product

Per group of 3–4 students

  • Clear cup or beaker of water with a pinch of baking soda (source of dissolved CO2)
  • Fresh leaves of a water plant such as Elodea, or spinach leaf discs (about 10 per group)
  • Lamp or bright window light, and a timer
  • Optional: 10 mL syringe for the leaf-disc version of the demonstration
  • “Photosynthesis Inputs & Outputs” sorting cards (printed and cut)
  • Observation sheet and pencil

Per student

  • Science notebook
  • Exit ticket (printed copy of the quiz below)

Timed Activity Schedule

TimeMinutesActivityDescriptionGrouping
0:00–0:088Hook & Prior KnowledgeAsk: “A tree grows from a tiny seed into a huge plant. Where does all that mass come from?” Students write a prediction in their notebooks, then share with a partner.Individual, then pairs
0:08–0:2012Direct InstructionIntroduce the word equation: carbon dioxide + water + light energy → glucose + oxygen. Use the diagram to show where each item enters or leaves the plant. Define chlorophyll, chloroplast and stomata.Whole class
0:20–0:4020Hands-On InvestigationGroups set up the leaf or Elodea demonstration in baking-soda water under a lamp, and observe oxygen bubbles or floating leaf discs. They record observations every 3–4 minutes and compare a “light” setup with a “dim/shaded” setup.Groups of 3–4
0:40–0:488Sorting Card ActivityGroups sort cards into “Inputs” and “Outputs” of photosynthesis, plus distractors (e.g., “soil,” “nitrogen”). They justify each choice.Same groups
0:48–0:535Debrief & ConnectionsDiscuss results. Revisit the hook question and revise predictions. Link to food chains and to the oxygen we breathe.Whole class

Total: 60 minutes

Teacher Notes

  • Key answer to the hook: Most of a plant’s mass comes from carbon dioxide in the air and water, not from soil. Many students expect “soil”, so revisit this at the end.
  • Common misconceptions:
    • “Plants get their food from the soil.” Soil supplies water and minerals, but the plant makes its own food.
    • “Photosynthesis is the plant’s way of breathing.” Plants also respire, day and night, and photosynthesis is a separate process.
    • “Chlorophyll is the food.” Chlorophyll absorbs light, and glucose is the food.
  • Demonstration set-up: Test the investigation the day before. Elodea produces visible bubbles within about 5 minutes under a strong lamp. If it is unavailable, use the leaf-disc method: remove air with a syringe so the discs sink, then time how long they take to rise in light.
  • Safety: Keep lamps away from water spills, and warn students that bulbs get hot. Remind them to wash their hands after handling plants.
  • Vocabulary support: Put the word equation where students can see it throughout the lesson. Use the terms reactant and product alongside “input” and “output”.
  • Assessment: Use the exit tickets to sort students into “secure”, “nearly there” and “needs reteach” for the next lesson. Question 4 reveals the most common misconception.
  • Extension to next lesson: Cellular respiration as the “reverse” process, and factors that affect the rate of photosynthesis.

Differentiation Tips

Support for students who need more help

  • Give a partially completed word equation with sentence starters or a word bank.
  • Use picture-labelled sorting cards and a diagram with arrows already drawn.
  • Assign structured roles in groups (materials manager, timer, recorder, reporter).
  • Allow oral responses or a read-aloud for the exit ticket.

Support for English language learners

  • Pre-teach key vocabulary with images and cognates (e.g., Spanish fotosíntesis, clorofila).
  • Let students label diagrams in their home language first, then in English.

Challenge for advanced learners

  • Introduce the balanced chemical equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O + light → C6H12O6 + 6O2.
  • Ask them to design a fair test of a second variable (light colour, distance from lamp, or CO2 concentration).
  • Have them explain why the leaf-disc results might vary and how to improve reliability.

Other supports

  • For students with visual or motor needs, pair them with a partner for set-up and use large-print or tactile cards.
  • Offer a choice of ways to show learning at the debrief: drawing, short paragraph, or verbal explanation.

Exit Ticket Quiz

Name: ______________________    Date: ______________

Circle the best answer for each question.

1. Which two substances does a plant need as raw materials for photosynthesis?

  1. Oxygen and glucose
  2. Carbon dioxide and water
  3. Nitrogen and soil
  4. Oxygen and water

2. What is the main product that the plant uses as food?

  1. Glucose
  2. Carbon dioxide
  3. Chlorophyll
  4. Oxygen

3. Which part of the plant cell contains chlorophyll and is where photosynthesis takes place?

  1. Nucleus
  2. Cell wall
  3. Chloroplast
  4. Vacuole

4. A student says, “Plants get most of their food from the soil.” Which response is the best correction?

  1. Correct, because roots take in sugar from the soil.
  2. Incorrect, because plants make their own food from carbon dioxide, water and light energy.
  3. Correct, because soil gives plants their energy from sunlight.
  4. Incorrect, because plants get their food from the air only, without water.

5. In the investigation, the plant under the bright lamp produced more bubbles than the plant in the shade. What does this suggest?

  1. Plants make oxygen only in the dark.
  2. Light has no effect on photosynthesis.
  3. More light can increase the rate of photosynthesis.
  4. Shade makes plants produce more glucose.

Answer Key

QuestionCorrect AnswerExplanation
1BCarbon dioxide and water are the reactants. Oxygen and glucose are products, and nitrogen and soil are not raw materials for photosynthesis.
2AGlucose is the sugar the plant makes and uses for energy and growth. Oxygen is a by-product released into the air.
3CChloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy.
4BPlants make their own food. Soil provides water and minerals, but not sugar or energy.
5CGreater bubble production (oxygen) under bright light suggests a higher rate of photosynthesis.

Interpreting the results

  • 5/5 or 4/5: Secure. Move on to extension tasks.
  • 3/5: Nearly there. Review with a short recap or a small-group check-in.
  • 2/5 or below: Reteach using the diagram and sorting cards. Check misconceptions, especially Question 4.
